analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare drug plans to let any qualified pharmacy join their networks, curbing pharmacy benefit managers.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing, a vote, or any action beyond its referral.
analysis.plain_summary: Pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) — middlemen that drug plans hire to build pharmacy networks — often exclude independent and community pharmacies unless they accept steep price cuts or steep fees. This bill would require Medicare drug plans and their PBMs to admit any pharmacy that meets standard contract terms, and would direct Medicare officials to define by 2026 what 'reasonable' contract terms mean. The aim is to keep neighborhood pharmacies in Medicare networks so beneficiaries can fill prescriptions close to home.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, especially in rural and underserved areas, gain more choice of where to fill prescriptions and a better chance their local pharmacy stays open. Independent and community pharmacies gain guaranteed access to Medicare drug-plan networks on terms an outside regulator deems reasonable.

how_it_helps.text: Medicare prescription drug plans and PBMs must allow any pharmacy that meets the plan's standard contract terms to join the network [S3].
Those contract terms must be 'reasonable and relevant,' with the Department of Health and Human Services required to set standards for reasonable terms by January 1, 2026 [S3].
The bill is framed as assuring pharmacy access and choice for Medicare beneficiaries [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers and the large insurers that own them lose a lever they use to steer prescriptions toward their own mail-order and specialty pharmacies and to squeeze independent pharmacies on reimbursement. Drug plans could face somewhat higher administrative and network costs.

drawbacks.text: The bill sets no reimbursement rates and does not cap what PBMs can pay pharmacies, so a pharmacy could be admitted to a network on terms that are procedurally 'reasonable' but still financially thin.

Requiring broader networks could raise drug plans' administrative costs, some of which could be passed into Medicare premiums or plan design, and broad networks can undercut plans' preferred-pharmacy arrangements that currently offer beneficiaries lower copays at select stores.
The government standards for 'reasonable' terms were not due until January 1, 2026, leaving years of ambiguity about what the requirement actually means in practice.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real and widely documented problem — pharmacy networks shrinking and independent pharmacies closing as PBMs consolidate control — but it is a narrow fix. It guarantees a seat at the table for qualified pharmacies without directly addressing reimbursement rates or PBM pricing practices, so its benefits to patients would likely be real but modest, and the main costs fall on the large PBMs and insurers that currently set the terms.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in July 2023, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Manchin introduced the bill on July 20, 2023, with Sen. Blackburn as the original Republican cosponsor [S1][S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance [S5].
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — appears in the action history for the remainder of the 118th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmacy benefit managers and the big insurers that own them keep control of Medicare pharmacy networks, and independent pharmacies and their patients get no relief.

for.name: Sen. Joe Manchin III
for.role: U.S. Senator from West Virginia; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require Medicare drug plans and PBMs to admit any qualified pharmacy on reasonable terms.

for.name: Sen. Marsha Blackburn
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, making it bipartisan from day one.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral in July 2023 and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan at introduction — a Democrat from West Virginia sponsored it with a Republican from Tennessee as cosponsor — but it never advanced far enough for a partisan floor fight to take shape.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers (the large PBM companies, e.g. the big three that process most Medicare drug claims)
industries.note: PBMs currently decide which pharmacies make it into Medicare networks and on what terms, which lets them steer volume to their own mail-order pharmacies and squeeze independents. The bill takes away that gatekeeping power and subjects their contracts to federal 'reasonable terms' standards [S2][S3].
The bill guarantees them a path into Medicare drug-plan networks if they meet standard terms, addressing network exclusions that have pushed many neighborhood pharmacies toward closure [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Medicare Part D drug-plan sponsors (large insurers)
industries.note: Plans lose some flexibility to build narrow preferred networks that steer beneficiaries and lower plan costs, but they are not the bill's main target and their PBM affiliates bear the more direct burden.
